title: Taking up the violin at twelve and the Flint citywide orchestra
summary: Inspired by a girl violinist in his father's choir, he got a violin and became second violin in a citywide orchestra in Flint, Michigan, but gave it up as too hard to master.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: Well, how old were you when you first started? When did you first start, with violin ?

Yes, that would come into the period when I was 12 years old. That's when I actually remember starting to play music, although I could play when I was five or six years old. I was always pluncking on the piano. And I
remember that. As I said, everybody in my family tells me how my mother used to hold me on her lap when she played.

But my official beginning of my knowledge of playing was at the age of 12, when I became interested in the violin. And there was a grown girl, I imagine she was perhaps 16 or 17 years old who played the violin in the church choir of my father's church. I believe that was Youngstown, Ohio, some city in Ohio, and I became interested in music through that source, the choir. I pumped the organ for the church, and in fact everybody in our family at some time or other had sang in the choir, and I eventually as a kid sang in the junior choir. I was always involved in the choir, and the music facilities of the church.

And -- but it was this interest that I heard from this violin played by this young girl that really got me interested in the violin, and I asked my father to buy a violin for me and he went and got me a violin. And I played it and I remember definitely I played it long enough to become a member of the citywide orchestra in Flint, Michigan.

I don't know the name but it was a city project at that time, which included young musicians from all of the schools, public schools in Flint, Michigan, and I don't know how, I was chosen. I remember I played second violin part. I don't think I was ever that good, but
evidently I must have been able to played in tune and read the notes to become a member of the citywide orchestra.

No, in fact that's why I stopped playing it. It was very difficult to really master the violin and I knew that and it gave me tone qualities. It was a life time job. Of course some people are gifted, and I think I must have been gifted to some degree. But I didn't have the mastery of fingering the instrument properly to completely get the sound that I thought was desirable. As I said, it must have been acceptable for the supervisor to choose me, you know. And I'm positive that I was able to play the notes, to read the notes properly and in tune.
